Record B keeps in place universal public health insurance with no patient charges and more generous unemployment and minimum income support, and it expanded dental coverage, whereas Record A voted to cut low-income health coverage and food assistance and against premium subsidy extensions.

Record B keeps in place a universal, free, tax-funded health service and a much stronger guaranteed minimum income (about 50% of median versus 6%), and it expands benefits through official acts, which outweighs Record A's opposition to cuts within a non-universal system that leaves about 8% of residents uninsured.

Record B keeps a far more generous income-support guarantee (about 39% vs 18% of median income for the minimum, plus higher pension and unemployment replacement) alongside universal compulsory health insurance, and it held pensions at 48% of wages, which outweighs its modest retrenchments relative to Record A's free-at-point-of-care health coverage and small dental and school-meal expansions.

Record A's official votes consistently defend and expand coverage and income support by opposing health and food-aid cuts and backing subsidy extensions, whereas Record B backs its more generous system only through influence-tier proposals, and its official acts are mixed: it opposed a budget that raised health spending and indexed benefits, and it backed an unemployment benefit cut.
